q: What is a Diagnosis-Related Group (DRG)?
r: A system that groups hospital cases with similar conditions and costs for payment
Medicare pays a set rate per group.
w: A group of doctors who share a clinic and split profits
A group of drugs that treat the same illness
A group of nurses assigned to one ward

q: Under a DRG payment, a hospital is paid a fixed amount for a stay. If the hospital's cost is below the amount, what happens?
r: The hospital keeps the difference as margin
w: The hospital must refund the difference

q: What is the Inpatient Prospective Payment System (IPPS)?
r: Medicare's system of paying hospitals set amounts per inpatient discharge
w: A system that pays doctors per visit only
A system that pays patients for staying

q: What is the Hospital Readmissions Reduction Program?
r: A Medicare program that reduces payments to hospitals with excess readmissions for certain conditions
w: A program that pays hospitals for more readmissions
A program that builds new hospitals

q: What is hospital value-based purchasing?
r: Adjusting Medicare payments based on quality and patient experience scores
w: Buying supplies at the lowest price only
Paying for the most services performed
Paying a fixed fee per patient

q: What is the outpatient prospective payment system (OPPS)?
r: Medicare's method of paying hospitals set rates for outpatient services

q: What is the 340B Drug Pricing Program?
r: A federal program that lets eligible safety-net providers buy outpatient drugs at discounts
w: A program that sets the price of all drugs
A program for patients to buy drugs online

q: What is charge capture?
r: Recording all billable services and supplies provided to a patient

q: What is a claim scrubber?
r: Software that checks claims for errors before they are submitted

q: What is a denial rate?
r: The share of submitted claims that payers refuse to pay
w: The share of patients who refuse care
The share of staff who refuse shifts

q: A clinic submits 1,000 claims and 80 are denied. What is the denial rate?
w: 80 percent, found by treating the count as a percent
0.8 percent, found by moving the decimal

q: What is net collection rate?
r: The share of the collectible amount that is actually collected
w: The share of patients who pay in cash

q: A practice's allowed charges are $200,000 and it collected $190,000. What is its net collection rate?
w: 105 percent, found by dividing allowed by collected

q: What is gross revenue versus net revenue in a hospital?
r: Gross is total billed charges; net is what is actually expected after contractual adjustments

q: What is a contractual adjustment?
r: The difference between a provider's charge and the amount the payer has agreed to allow
Written off, not billed to the patient.
w: A bonus paid by an insurer
A fine charged to a hospital

q: A hospital charges $5,000 for a service and the payer's contract allows $3,200. What is the contractual adjustment?
What is a payer mix?
r: The proportion of a provider's revenue from each type of payer, such as Medicare, Medicaid and commercial insurers

q: Why is a hospital with a high share of Medicaid and uninsured patients often under more financial pressure?
r: Those payers typically pay less than the cost of care or nothing at all
w: Those payers pay the highest rates

q: What is price transparency in healthcare?
r: Requirements that providers make the prices of services publicly available

q: What is a good faith estimate?
r: A provider's estimate of expected charges for a service given to an uninsured or self-pay patient
w: A promise of payment by the patient

q: What is financial counseling for patients?
r: Helping patients understand bills, payment options and financial assistance

q: What is productivity measured as worked hours per patient day used for?
r: Comparing staffing levels with patient volume

q: A unit worked 1,200 hours in a month and had 400 patient days. What are its worked hours per patient day?
A department has 8 full-time employees and 4 half-time employees. How many FTEs does it have?
A hospital's labor cost is $6 million on revenue of $20 million. What share of revenue is labor?
w: 70 percent, which is the share not spent on labor
3.3 percent, found by inverting and moving the decimal

q: What is a flexible budget?
r: A budget that adjusts for actual activity levels
w: A budget made by a gymnast

q: What is a zero-based budget?
r: A budget in which every expense must be justified from scratch each period
w: A budget that begins with last year's amounts

q: What is a rolling forecast?
r: A forecast updated regularly to look a set period ahead
w: A forecast made once and never changed

q: What is days cash on hand?
r: How many days a hospital could pay its operating expenses using its cash
w: The number of days patients stay

q: A hospital has $30 million in cash and daily cash operating expenses of $300,000. How many days cash on hand does it have?
What is a hospital's bond rating?
r: An assessment of its ability to repay debt

q: What is a hospitalist?
r: A physician who focuses on caring for patients in the hospital

q: What is an intensivist?
r: A physician who specializes in caring for critically ill patients in intensive care
w: A physician who treats only skin conditions
A physician who works in a pharmacy

q: What is a case manager?
r: A professional who coordinates a patient's care and services across providers

q: What is utilization review?
r: Evaluating whether services are medically necessary and appropriate
Used to control cost and quality.

q: What is discharge planning?
r: Preparing a patient to leave the hospital with needed follow-up care and services

q: What is a care transition?
r: A patient's move from one care setting to another, such as hospital to home

q: What are social determinants of health?
r: Non-medical factors such as housing, income and education that influence health

q: What is population health management?
r: Improving the health of a defined group through data, prevention and coordinated care
w: Counting the population of a city
Treating one patient at a time only

q: What is a community health center?
r: A nonprofit clinic that provides primary care in underserved areas, often on a sliding fee scale
w: A hospital for the wealthy only

q: What is a rural health clinic?
r: A clinic in a rural area that serves patients and may receive special Medicare and Medicaid payment

q: What is a skilled nursing facility (SNF)?
r: A facility offering short-term nursing and rehabilitation care after a hospital stay
Often covered for a limited time by Medicare.

q: What is assisted living?
r: Housing with help for daily activities for people who need some support

q: What is a rehabilitation hospital?
r: A hospital that helps patients recover function after illness or injury

q: What is an academic medical center?
r: A hospital affiliated with a medical school that combines care, teaching and research

q: What is a trauma center?
r: A hospital equipped to care for severely injured patients around the clock

q: What is a Level I trauma center?
r: The highest level of trauma care, with comprehensive services and research
w: A care center for minor injuries

q: What is a patient flow problem in an emergency department?
r: Delays caused by bottlenecks in moving patients through triage, treatment and admission

q: What is boarding in an emergency department?
r: Holding admitted patients in the ED because no inpatient bed is available

q: What is bed management?
r: Coordinating patient placement and availability of beds

q: What is materials management in a hospital?
r: Ordering, storing and distributing supplies and equipment

q: What is a par level in supply management?
r: The minimum quantity of an item to keep on hand before reordering
w: The golf score of a nurse

q: What is a group purchasing organization (GPO)?
r: An entity that negotiates lower prices for supplies on behalf of many hospitals

q: What is CLIA?
r: The federal program that sets quality standards for clinical laboratory testing

q: What does environmental services (housekeeping) do in a hospital?
r: Cleans and disinfects rooms to prevent infection

q: What does dietary (nutrition) services do?
r: Plans and prepares meals that meet patients' dietary needs

q: What does a respiratory therapist do?
r: Helps patients with breathing problems, including using ventilators and oxygen

q: What does a physical therapist do?
r: Helps patients restore movement and manage pain through exercise and treatment

q: What does an occupational therapist do?
r: Helps patients regain skills for daily living and work
w: Treats only job injuries by surgery

q: What does a social worker do in a hospital?
r: Helps patients and families with resources, planning and coping

q: What does a health information manager oversee?
r: The quality, security and accessibility of patient health records
Includes coding and release of information.

q: What does a medical coder do?
r: Translates medical documentation into standard codes for billing and data

q: What does a patient access representative do?
r: Registers patients, verifies insurance and collects information at admission

q: What are the Medicare Conditions of Participation?
r: Federal health and safety standards that hospitals must meet to take part in Medicare

q: What are National Patient Safety Goals?
r: Joint Commission requirements to prevent common patient safety problems

q: Why must staff use two patient identifiers before giving medication?
r: To make sure the right patient receives the right treatment

q: What is a hospital-acquired infection (HAI)?
r: An infection a patient develops during a hospital stay that was not present on admission
w: An infection a patient has when arriving
An infection spread among staff only

q: What is the single most effective way to prevent infection spread in healthcare?
What is a central line-associated bloodstream infection (CLABSI)?
r: A serious infection linked to a central venous catheter
Hospitals track and work to prevent it.

q: What is a never event in healthcare?
r: A serious, largely preventable error such as surgery on the wrong body part

q: What is a sentinel event?
r: An unexpected event that causes death or serious harm to a patient

q: What is a near miss?
r: An error that was caught before reaching the patient
w: A mistake that harmed a patient

q: Why should near misses be reported?
r: They reveal weaknesses so that harm can be prevented

q: What is a culture of safety?
r: An environment where staff report problems freely and learn from them

q: What is the purpose of a medication reconciliation process?
r: To compare a patient's medication lists at transitions to avoid errors

q: What are the 'five rights' of medication administration?
r: Right patient, drug, dose, route and time
w: Right color, shape, size, smell and taste
Right doctor, nurse, aide, clerk and guard
Right price, brand, store, bag and receipt

q: What is the role of an institutional review board (IRB)?
r: To review research involving people to protect participants' rights and welfare

q: What is the HITECH Act?
r: A law that promoted adoption of electronic health records and strengthened HIPAA enforcement

q: What is the HIPAA Breach Notification Rule?
r: A rule requiring covered entities to notify affected people and regulators after a breach of unsecured PHI
w: A rule that forbids notifying anyone

q: What is the minimum necessary standard under HIPAA?
r: Using or sharing only the least amount of PHI needed for a purpose

q: What is a business associate agreement (BAA)?
r: A contract requiring a vendor that handles PHI to protect it as HIPAA requires
Signed between covered entity and vendor.
w: A contract to sell a business

q: What is the Controlled Substances Act?
r: A federal law that regulates the making, distribution and use of certain drugs

q: Which drug schedule includes drugs with no accepted medical use and high abuse potential?
What does the DEA do in healthcare?
r: Enforces controlled-substance laws and registers prescribers

q: What does the FDA regulate?
r: The safety and effectiveness of drugs, devices and food

q: What is the role of state medical boards?
What is the National Practitioner Data Bank?
r: A federal database that tracks malpractice payments and certain adverse actions against practitioners

q: What is the Good Samaritan law?
r: A law that protects people who give reasonable emergency help from liability

q: What is vicarious liability?
r: An employer's responsibility for the acts of employees done within their work
w: An employee's liability for the employer's debts

q: What is a statute of limitations in a malpractice case?
r: The time limit within which a claim must be filed
w: A limit on the number of patients

q: What is the difference between a patient's capacity and competence?
r: Capacity is the clinical ability to make a specific decision; competence is a legal determination
w: Capacity is legal; competence is medical

q: If a patient lacks capacity and has no advance directive, who usually makes decisions?
r: A legally authorized surrogate, often a family member

q: What is a living will?
r: A document stating a person's wishes about treatment if they cannot speak for themselves
w: A will that gives away property

q: What is a POLST form?
r: A medical order that records a seriously ill patient's treatment wishes

r: A database that links each patient to a unique identifier across a health system

q: What problem can a duplicate medical record cause?
r: Incomplete information that could harm a patient

r: To collect demographic, contact and insurance information

q: What is wave scheduling?
r: Booking several patients at the start of each hour and seeing them in order of arrival

q: What is open-access (same-day) scheduling?
r: Keeping slots open so patients can be seen the day they call

q: What is the best way to handle a patient who arrives 30 minutes late?
r: Follow clinic policy: see them if possible or reschedule politely
